section_summary: This section concludes the dispute over an Osaka Mainichi propaganda pamphlet that falsely attributed pro-Japanese remarks about North China to U.S. Military Attaché William C. Crane. Most of the section documents British diplomatic protests against Japanese military and postal interference with the Tsingtao Times, Peking and Tientsin Times, and other British newspapers circulating in North China. The correspondence traces the dispute from August 1938 through February 1939, ending with a Japanese denial of formal restrictions while acknowledging that newspapers might have been detained temporarily or mistaken for the banned Peking and Tientsin Times.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 2724 concerning false statements attributed to Lieutenant Colonel Crane
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports that an Osaka Mainichi propaganda pamphlet falsely attributed pro-Japanese statements about North China to former Military Attaché William C. Crane.
subfiles.summary: Grew says Lt. Col. Crane categorically denied remarks attributed to him, which drew attention in Hong Kong, Shanghai and Tokyo; he raised it informally with Hirota as a breach of press ethics and injustice, and Hirota promised steps; Crane's letter, conversation memo and clipping enclosed.

subfiles.title: Crane's letter to the editor of the Osaka Mainichi
subfiles.about: Requests that the Osaka Mainichi omit comments falsely attributed to Crane concerning the restoration of order in North China.
subfiles.summary: Crane writes the Osaka Mainichi editor that the Japan Advertiser announced a holiday pamphlet with supposed comments by him; he denies speaking to any press representative about restoring order and asks they not be published.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Grew's conversation with Foreign Minister Hirota
subfiles.about: Records Grew's informal protest over the publication of statements falsely attributed to Crane in the pamphlet Commonsense and the China Emergency.
subfiles.summary: Grew showed Hirota the Osaka Mainichi pamphlet and Crane's denial, calling it flagrant disregard of press ethics, an injustice to Crane and propaganda likely spread in the U.S.; Hirota read the remarks and promised action.

subfiles.title: Merry Christmas—Domei States the Case for Japan
subfiles.about: Describes a Domei holiday propaganda booklet defending Japan's conduct in China and quoting Crane and Franklin Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Domei circulated a Christmas booklet, "Commonsense and the China Emergency," attacking Chinese warlords and Communism and denying Japanese territorial ambitions, falsely quoting Crane dismissing Chinese propaganda and invoking Roosevelt's quarantine language to argue China should be isolated.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for General Araki's Japan Advertiser interview
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a despatch about General Araki's interview with Japan Advertiser representative Frank Hedges and the resulting difficulties and threats.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Tokyo despatch 2798 on General Araki's February 3, 1938 Japan Advertiser interview with Frank Hedges, which led to threats; clippings enclosed.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Tokyo despatch no. 3253
subfiles.about: Summarizes British complaints about Japanese interference with the Tsingtao Times and Peking and Tientsin Times.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs notes despatch 3253 enclosed British representations for the Tsingtao Times and against the Peking and Tientsin Times ban, a serious interference with British interests; no State action needed.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3253 transmitting British complaints about newspaper distribution
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits two British letters concerning Japanese interference with British newspapers published in North China.
subfiles.summary: Grew sends copies of the British Ambassador's September 15 and 19 letters to Japan's Vice-Minister on restrictions on distributing British newspapers in North China.

subfiles.title: Craigie to Horinouchi concerning the Tsingtao Times
subfiles.about: Forwards the British Ambassador to China's account of interference with the Tsingtao Times and asks that further interference be prevented.
subfiles.summary: Craigie refers to Horinouchi's August 15 letter and sends Clark Kerr's communication to Tani on obstacles to distributing the Tsingtao Times, requesting assurances protecting its employees.

subfiles.title: Clark Kerr to Tani concerning mistreatment of Tsingtao Times employees
subfiles.about: Disputes Japanese claims that interference with Tsingtao Times delivery had ceased and requests guarantees against further abuse.
subfiles.summary: Clark Kerr says the paper stopped using Chinese messengers without safety assurances, that four Japanese gendarmes abducted a Chinese employee May 17 and beat him over three days, and asks Tani for assurances against recurrence.

subfiles.title: Craigie to Horinouchi protesting the ban on the Peking and Tientsin Times
subfiles.about: Requests the lifting of a Japanese ban on the Peking and Tientsin Times.
subfiles.summary: Craigie protests Japan's ban on the Peking and Tientsin Times, with censors stopping even first-class copies to subscribers, an unfavorable response expected, and calls it serious interference with British interests in North China.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Tokyo despatch no. 3298
subfiles.about: Summarizes continued Japanese obstruction of the Peking and Tientsin Times despite British protests.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs notes the ban continues, postal workers must reject copies addressed to individuals, and despatch 3298 enclosed a British memorandum; no action requested.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3298 transmitting a British memorandum on continued interference
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a British memorandum documenting continued Japanese interference with British newspaper distribution.
subfiles.summary: Grew, after despatch 3253, sends a September 28 British Embassy memorandum to Japan's Foreign Office presenting continuing restrictions as interference with British rights in North China.

subfiles.title: British Embassy memorandum on the continuing Peking and Tientsin Times ban
subfiles.about: States that the ban on the Peking and Tientsin Times remained in force and had expanded to copies addressed to diplomatic personnel.
subfiles.summary: British memorandum recalls Craigie's September 19 request, reports no improvement, and says postal employees were ordered to refuse copies addressed to individuals in Peking embassies and legations.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3413 transmitting further British communications
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a British note verbale reviewing the newspaper dispute and a formal protest to the Japanese Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards two further British communications concerning Japanese interference with British newspaper distribution in North China. The first is an undated case history apparently delivered to the Vice-Minister on October 28. The second is Craigie's formal protest of November 2 to Foreign Minister Arita.

subfiles.title: British note verbale reviewing the Peking and Tientsin Times dispute
subfiles.about: Reviews unsuccessful British efforts to obtain the unconditional removal of the Peking and Tientsin Times ban.
subfiles.summary: British note reviews Craigie's talks with Horinouchi, September 19 to October 14: Japan would lift the ban only if the paper accepted conditions, Craigie demanded unconditional removal, and postal authorities hadn't been told to ease diplomatic copies; apparently handed over October 28, 1938.

subfiles.title: British formal protest against the Peking and Tientsin Times ban
subfiles.about: Formally protests the Japanese ban on the Peking and Tientsin Times and demands restoration of free circulation.
subfiles.summary: Craigie protests that local authorities exceeded their powers, damaged British-Japanese relations, and cited no recent objectionable content; Britain rejects conditions for lifting the ban and especially protests interception of copies for diplomatic and consular officials.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3524 transmitting Dodds's letter on broader newspaper interference
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a further British communication about Japanese interference with newspapers in North China.
subfiles.summary: Grew, after despatch 3413, forwards a December 2 letter from British Counsellor J. L. Dodds to Sho Kurihara reporting interference had continued and broadened beyond the Peking and Tientsin Times.

subfiles.title: Dodds to Kurihara concerning expanding interference with British newspapers
subfiles.about: Renews the demand to lift the Peking and Tientsin Times ban and reports detention of several other British newspapers at Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: Dodds is surprised Japan hadn't acted on Britain's November 2 protest, reporting November 5-19 issues of the North China Daily News, Shanghai Times and Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury were detained at Tianjin, most never delivered, and asks an end to the ban and wider interference.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Tokyo despatch no. 3704
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Japanese response to British allegations that newspapers had been seized by the Tianjin postal administration.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs notes the Japanese Foreign Office denied seizing the North China Daily News and Shanghai Times in November, but postal officials were cautioned as they may have confused them with the Peking and Tientsin Times.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3704 transmitting the Japanese Foreign Office response
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a translated Japanese Foreign Office note responding to British complaints about newspaper restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Grew refers to his December 21 despatch on British protests over interference with newspaper distribution in North China. He encloses the February 10 Japanese note, which denies that special prohibitory restrictions had been imposed but says the attention of postal authorities had been drawn to the issue.

subfiles.title: Kurihara to Dodds denying formal restrictions on British newspapers
subfiles.about: Denies that the Tianjin postal administration formally prohibited the named British newspapers while conceding possible temporary detention or mistaken identification.
subfiles.summary: Kurihara says inquiries found no special restrictions on mailing the North China Daily News, Shanghai Times and others, though copies might have been provisionally held for prohibited propaganda or confused with the Peking and Tientsin Times; postal authorities were told.
